title: Atypical Pneumonia and Pneumonia in Immunocompromised

questions.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
questions.q: Mycoplasma is described as the smallest free living organism capable of ______.
opts: sporulation
photosynthesis
replication
motility
questions.exp: The opening line reads 'Smallest free living organism capable of replication', the superlative that anchors the whole mycoplasma section. (Book p286)

questions.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
questions.q: Which three structural facts explain why β-lactams fail in mycoplasma?
opts: There is no cell wall, β-lactams are therefore not effective, and sterols are present while flagella are absent
There is no cell wall, β-lactams are effective through porins, and sterols are present with flagella absent
There is a thick cell wall, β-lactams are therefore effective, and sterols are absent
There is no cell wall, β-lactams are therefore not effective, and sterols are absent with flagella present
questions.exp: The block reads 'No cell wall: β-lactams not effective, Sterols present' and 'No flagella', so the missing wall both excludes β-lactams and requires sterols in the membrane. (Book p286)

questions.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
questions.q: Which two diseases are listed under mycoplasma, and how is it transmitted?
opts: Pharyngitis and bronchiolitis in 10%, transmitted by direct contact
Lobar pneumonia and empyema, transmitted by droplet infection
Tracheobronchitis or pharyngitis and pneumonia in 50%, transmitted by the faecal–oral route
Tracheobronchitis or pharyngitis and pneumonia in 10%, transmitted by droplet infection
questions.exp: The disease list gives tracheobronchitis/pharyngitis and 'Pneumonia (10%)', followed by 'Transmission: Droplet infection'. (Book p286)

questions.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
questions.q: Which four features describe the pneumonia of mycoplasma on page 286?
opts: Low grade fever, dry cough, hemoptysis and consolidation with bronchial breathing
Low grade fever, cough, scanty sputum and a paucity of clinical signs
High grade fever, cough, copious purulent sputum and florid clinical signs
High spiking fever, pleuritic pain, scanty sputum and a paucity of clinical signs
questions.exp: The four bullets under pneumonia read 'Low grade fever', 'Cough', 'Scanty sputum' and 'Paucity of clinical signs' — the dissociation between symptoms and signs is the point. (Book p286)

questions.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
questions.q: Match each mycoplasma extrapulmonary manifestation to its printed wording — 1) Hematological 2) Dermatological 3) Neurological … A) Steven Johnson syndrome (SJS)/erythema multiforme B) Guillain Barre syndrome (GBS) C) Cold antibody autoimmune hemolytic anemia (IgM)
questions.exp: The list prints cold antibody autoimmune hemolytic anemia (IgM), SJS/erythema multiforme and GBS, before encephalitis, bullous myringitis, myocarditis/pericarditis and arthralgia with adenopathy. (Book p286)

questions.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
questions.q: Which four radiological patterns are printed for mycoplasma on page 286?
opts: Reticulonodular consolidation starting at the hilum, cavitation, ground glass appearance and tree in bud appearance
Lobar consolidation with air bronchogram, interstitial involvement, ground glass appearance and tree in bud appearance
Reticulonodular or patchy consolidation starting at the hilum, interstitial involvement, ground glass appearance and tree in bud appearance in endobronchial inflammation or obstruction
Reticulonodular or patchy consolidation starting at the base, interstitial involvement, ground glass appearance and honeycomb change
questions.exp: The imaging bullets read reticulonodular/patchy consolidation starting at the hilum, interstitial involvement, ground glass appearance and tree in bud appearance in endobronchial inflammation/obstruction. (Book p286)

questions.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
questions.q: Match each mycoplasma culture detail to its printed description — 1) Medium 2) Method 3) Appearance … A) Biphasic with fried egg appearance B) PPLO agar C) Diene's method
questions.exp: The culture block reads 'PPLO agar: Diene's method' and 'Biphasic with fried egg appearance', the fried egg colony being the classic description. (Book p286)

questions.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
questions.q: Which diagnostic test is bracketed as rapid and most sensitive, and which drug is the printed drug of choice?
opts: PCR of respiratory secretion and culture are rapid and most sensitive, and a respiratory quinolone is the drug of choice
PCR of respiratory secretion and serology are rapid and most sensitive, and erythromycin is the drug of choice
Culture and serology are rapid and most sensitive, and doxycycline is the drug of choice
PCR of respiratory secretion and serology are rapid and most sensitive, and azithromycin is the drug of choice
questions.exp: The bracket joins 'PCR of respiratory secretion' and 'Serology' under 'Rapid & most sensitive', and the treatment list starts 'Azithromycin (DOC)' followed by doxycycline and respiratory quinolones. (Book p286)

questions.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
questions.q: Mycoplasma injures epithelium through hydrogen peroxide and ______ produced by the organism.
opts: nitric oxide
peroxynitrite
hydroxyl radical
superoxide
questions.exp: The pathogen line reads 'Hydrogen peroxide & superoxide produced by organism → Epithelial cell injury', with prognosis printed as good. (Book p286)

questions.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
questions.q: A 22-year-old student has a week of low grade fever and dry cough with scanty sputum and almost no chest signs; cold agglutinins are positive. Which organism and drug of choice does the page support?
opts: Chlamydia, treated with azithromycin
Mycoplasma, treated with a sulfonamide
Legionella, treated with azithromycin and rifampicin
Mycoplasma, treated with azithromycin
questions.exp: Mycoplasma gives low grade fever, cough, scanty sputum and a paucity of signs with cold antibody autoimmune hemolysis, and azithromycin is printed as DOC. (Book p286)

questions.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three are printed extrapulmonary manifestations of mycoplasma, one belongs to chlamydia:
opts: Atherosclerosis
Arthralgia with adenopathy
Bullous myringitis
Encephalitis
questions.exp: The mycoplasma list prints cold antibody hemolysis, SJS, GBS, encephalitis, bullous myringitis, myocarditis/pericarditis and arthralgia with adenopathy; atherosclerosis is the single extrapulmonary manifestation given for chlamydia. (Book p286)

questions.sec: Chlamydia as an Obligate Intracellular Peptidoglycan-Free Bacterium with Its Elementary Body, Walking Pneumonia, HEp-2 Isolation and Micro-Immunofluorescence, plus the Legionella Phenotype
questions.q: Which four features define chlamydia as printed on page 287?
opts: Obligate intracellular bacterium, thick peptidoglycan, human to human transmission and an elementary body that is metabolically inactive
Obligate intracellular bacterium, absence of peptidoglycan, zoonotic transmission and a reticulate body that is the infective form
Obligate intracellular bacterium, absence of peptidoglycan, human to human transmission and an elementary body that is extracellular, metabolically inactive and infective
Facultative intracellular bacterium, presence of peptidoglycan, human to human transmission and an elementary body that is metabolically active
questions.exp: The bullets read 'Obligate intracellular bacteria', 'Absence of peptidoglycan', 'Human to human transmission' and 'elementary body: Extracellular, metabolically inactive, infective form'. (Book p287)

questions.sec: Chlamydia as an Obligate Intracellular Peptidoglycan-Free Bacterium with Its Elementary Body, Walking Pneumonia, HEp-2 Isolation and Micro-Immunofluorescence, plus the Legionella Phenotype
questions.q: The chlamydial elementary body is extracellular, metabolically inactive and ______.
opts: infective
non-infective
replicating
adherent
questions.exp: The elementary body bullet reads 'Extracellular, metabolically inactive, infective form', the dormant but transmissible stage. (Book p287)

questions.sec: Chlamydia as an Obligate Intracellular Peptidoglycan-Free Bacterium with Its Elementary Body, Walking Pneumonia, HEp-2 Isolation and Micro-Immunofluorescence, plus the Legionella Phenotype
questions.q: Which clinical features of chlamydia are printed on page 287?
opts: A prolonged asymptomatic condition of the upper respiratory tract, atypical pneumonia in 10% and lobar pneumonia with copious sputum

A prolonged asymptomatic condition of the upper respiratory tract, atypical pneumonia in 10% and walking pneumonia indistinguishable from mycoplasma, with low grade fever, minimal sputum and dry cough
A prolonged symptomatic condition of the upper respiratory tract, atypical pneumonia in 10% and walking pneumonia indistinguishable from legionella
A short symptomatic condition of the lower respiratory tract, atypical pneumonia in 50% and lobar pneumonia distinguishable from mycoplasma
questions.exp: The block reads 'Prolonged asymptomatic condition of upper respiratory tract', 'Atypical pneumonia (10%)', 'Walking pneumonia (cannot differentiate from mycoplasma)' and the nonspecific trio of low grade fever, minimal sputum and dry cough. (Book p287)

questions.sec: Chlamydia as an Obligate Intracellular Peptidoglycan-Free Bacterium with Its Elementary Body, Walking Pneumonia, HEp-2 Isolation and Micro-Immunofluorescence, plus the Legionella Phenotype
questions.q: Which investigation is the gold standard for chlamydia, and which finding is expressly denied?
opts: Culture on PPLO agar is the gold standard, and there is no lobar consolidation
Isolation by HEp-2 cells is the gold standard, and there is lobar consolidation
Micro immunofluorescence serology is the gold standard, and there is no lobar consolidation
Micro immunofluorescence serology is the gold standard, and there is lobar consolidation
questions.exp: The investigation list reads isolation by HEp-2 cells, 'Serology: micro immuno fluorescence (Gold standard)' and 'No lobar consolidation'. (Book p287)

questions.sec: Chlamydia as an Obligate Intracellular Peptidoglycan-Free Bacterium with Its Elementary Body, Walking Pneumonia, HEp-2 Isolation and Micro-Immunofluorescence, plus the Legionella Phenotype
questions.q: Which drug is chlamydia expressly resistant to, and which two drugs are printed for it?
opts: It is resistant to penicillin, and azithromycin and doxycycline are used
It is resistant to sulfonamide, and azithromycin and doxycycline are used
It is resistant to azithromycin, and sulfonamide and doxycycline are used
It is resistant to doxycycline, and azithromycin and sulfonamide are used
questions.exp: The treatment block reads 'Resistant to sulfonamide' and 'Azithromycin, doxycycline', in deliberate contrast with mycoplasma's azithromycin, doxycycline and quinolones. (Book p287)

questions.sec: Chlamydia as an Obligate Intracellular Peptidoglycan-Free Bacterium with Its Elementary Body, Walking Pneumonia, HEp-2 Isolation and Micro-Immunofluorescence, plus the Legionella Phenotype
questions.q: Match each Legionella feature to its printed description — 1) Gram status 2) Oxygen requirement 3) Motility 4) Staining … A) Strict aerobes B) Gram negative, predominantly intracellular C) Partially acid fast D) Motile
questions.exp: The Legionella bullets read gram negative and predominantly intracellular, strict aerobes, motile and partially acid fast, before the aquatic reservoir and biofilm lines. (Book p287)

questions.sec: Chlamydia as an Obligate Intracellular Peptidoglycan-Free Bacterium with Its Elementary Body, Walking Pneumonia, HEp-2 Isolation and Micro-Immunofluorescence, plus the Legionella Phenotype
questions.q: The most pathogenic Legionella serovar is type ______.
questions.exp: The virulence bullet reads 'Type 1 serovar: most pathogenic', with 'Type 4 secretion system' given as the pathogenic factor. (Book p287)

questions.sec: Chlamydia as an Obligate Intracellular Peptidoglycan-Free Bacterium with Its Elementary Body, Walking Pneumonia, HEp-2 Isolation and Micro-Immunofluorescence, plus the Legionella Phenotype
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about chlamydia on page 287.
opts: False — it is an extracellular organism transmitted from animals
True — it lacks peptidoglycan and is resistant to sulfonamide
True — it has a thick peptidoglycan wall and is resistant to sulfonamide
False — it lacks peptidoglycan and is highly sensitive to sulfonamide
questions.exp: The chlamydia bullets read 'Absence of peptidoglycan' and, under treatment, 'Resistant to sulfonamide' with azithromycin or doxycycline used instead. (Book p287)

questions.sec: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
questions.q: Which route of Legionella transmission is printed first, and which comes second?
opts: Direct inoculation first, then microaspiration
Aerosolization first, then microaspiration
Microaspiration first, then aerosolization
Faecal–oral first, then aerosolization
questions.exp: The line reads 'Mode of transmission: microaspiration > Aerosolization', the greater-than sign ranking the two routes. (Book p288)

questions.sec: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
questions.q: Which medium is specific for Legionella, and what does the abbreviation stand for?
opts: BCYE medium, buffered charcoal yeast extract medium
BCYE medium, buffered cysteine yeast extract medium
BCYE medium, blood charcoal yeast extract medium
PPLO agar, pleuropneumonia-like organism agar
questions.exp: The culture line reads 'BCYE medium: Buffered charcoal yeast extract medium: Specific medium', the letters BCYE being the tested part. (Book p288)

questions.sec: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
questions.q: What does Gram staining of respiratory secretions show in Legionella infection?
opts: Gram-positive diplococci in chains with a background of pus cells
Pus cells and neutrophils are present with abundant gram-negative bacilli
No pus cells are seen but the organisms stain readily
Pus cells and neutrophils are present but no organisms are seen
questions.exp: The Gram staining findings read 'Pus cells, neutrophils +' and 'No organisms seen', the notorious sterile-looking Gram stain of legionellosis. (Book p288)

questions.sec: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
questions.q: Which four risk factors are printed for Legionella?
opts: Poor CMI, alcohol use, immunosuppression and hairy cell leukemia
Poor CMI, cigarette smoking, immunosuppression and hairy cell leukemia
Diabetes, cigarette smoking, immunosuppression and hairy cell leukemia
Poor CMI, cigarette smoking, immunosuppression and chronic kidney disease
questions.exp: The risk list reads 'Poor CMI', 'Cigarette smoking', 'Immunosuppression' and 'Hairy cell leukemia'. (Book p288)

questions.sec: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
questions.q: Match the typical and atypical Legionella pictures as printed — 1) Typical 2) Atypical … A) Non-productive cough, diarrhea, hyponatremia, elevated LFT, thrombocytopenia and hematuria B) Rapidly progressive, high grade fever, bilateral dense consolidation and leucocytosis
questions.exp: The typical arm is rapidly progressive with high grade fever, bilateral dense consolidation and leucocytosis; the atypical arm carries non-productive cough, GI symptoms, hyponatremia, elevated LFT, thrombocytopenia and hematuria. (Book p288)

questions.sec: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
questions.q: Match each Legionella syndrome to its severity — 1) Mild 2) Severe … A) Legionnaires disease B) Pontiac fever
questions.exp: The severity branch reads mild → Pontiac fever and severe → Legionnaires disease, in that order. (Book p288)

questions.sec: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
questions.q: Which three diagnostic statements are printed for Legionella on page 288?
opts: DFAT and urinary antigen testing both have high specificity, and sputum testing is the test of choice
DFAT has low specificity, urinary antigen has high specificity, and sputum testing is the test of choice
DFAT and urinary antigen testing both have low specificity, while sputum and aspiration testing are not done
DFAT and urinary antigen testing both have high specificity, while sputum and aspiration testing are not done
questions.exp: The diagnosis block reads 'DFAT: Direct fluorescence antibody test, High specificity', 'urinary antigen testing: High specificity' and 'Sputum/aspiration testing: Not done'. (Book p288)

questions.sec: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
questions.q: The treatment printed for Legionella is azithromycin, the drug of choice, combined with ______.
opts: rifampicin
ceftriaxone
clindamycin
cotrimoxazole
questions.exp: The treatment line reads 'Azithromycin (DOC) + Rifampicin', with quinolones as the alternative below it. (Book p288)

questions.sec: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
questions.q: A returning cruise passenger has high fever, diarrhea and hyponatremia with bilateral dense consolidation. Which organism and regimen does page 288 suggest?
opts: Legionella, treated with a sulfonamide
Mycoplasma, treated with azithromycin plus rifampicin
Legionella, treated with azithromycin plus rifampicin
Chlamydia, treated with azithromycin plus rifampicin
questions.exp: Cruise travel points to Legionella in the etiology table, the atypical picture prints diarrhea and hyponatremia, and treatment is 'Azithromycin (DOC) + Rifampicin'. (Book p288)

questions.sec: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
questions.q: A respiratory sample in a suspected Legionella case shows numerous pus cells and neutrophils but no organisms on Gram stain. How does the page explain this?
opts: The sample must have been taken after antibiotics, which always sterilises the stain
The finding excludes Legionella and points to mycoplasma
The finding is diagnostic of Nocardia, which is not seen on Gram stain
The Gram stain is characteristically negative for organisms even with abundant pus cells
questions.exp: The Gram staining findings read 'Pus cells, neutrophils +' and 'No organisms seen', which is why DFAT and urinary antigen are used instead. (Book p288)

questions.sec: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture
questions.q: Match each cause of lung abscess to its printed organisms — 1) Necrotising pneumonia 2) Aspiration pneumonia … A) Anaerobes B) Staphylococcus and Klebsiella
questions.exp: Necrotising pneumonia is a complication of pneumonia caused by staphylococcus and klebsiella, while aspiration pneumonia is anaerobic and presents with chronic symptoms. (Book p289)

questions.sec: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture
questions.q: Which two organisms are printed as causes of necrotising pneumonia?
opts: Staphylococcus and Pseudomonas
Staphylococcus and Klebsiella
Pneumococcus and Klebsiella
Klebsiella and Burkholderia
questions.exp: The necrotising pneumonia branch lists 'Staphylococcus' and 'Klebsiella' under organisms involved. (Book p289)

questions.sec: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture
questions.q: Which aspiration sites are printed, and in which order of frequency?
opts: Anterior segment of the upper lobe, more often than the basal segments of the lower lobe
Superior segment of the lower lobe, more often than the posterior segment of the upper lobe
Posterior segment of the upper lobe, more often than the superior segment of the lower lobe
Posterior segment of the lower lobe, more often than the superior segment of the upper lobe
questions.exp: The aspiration branch reads 'Site: Posterior segment of upper lobe > Superior segment of lower lobe', the greater-than sign giving the order. (Book p289)

questions.sec: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture
questions.q: Which five-step pathogenesis sequence is printed for lung abscess?
opts: Consolidation plus suppuration plus necrosis → fibrosis → drains into bronchus → purulent expectoration → abscess with air fluid level
Consolidation plus cavitation → rupture of abscess → drains into the pleural space → empyema → abscess with air fluid level
Suppuration plus necrosis → rupture of abscess → drains into bronchus → hemoptysis → abscess with air fluid level
Consolidation plus suppuration plus necrosis → rupture of abscess → drains into bronchus → purulent expectoration → abscess with air fluid level
questions.exp: The flow reads 'Consolidation + Suppuration + Necrosis → Rupture of abscess → Drains into bronchus → Purulent expectoration → Abscess with air fluid level'. (Book p289)

questions.sec: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture
questions.q: The most common site of a lung abscess is the posterior segment of the right ______ lobe.
opts: lingular
lower
middle
upper

questions.sec: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture

Toxicity is unaffected by drainage, and the cough produces purulent sputum
Toxicity decreases when the abscess drains into the pleural space, and the cough produces blood
Toxicity increases when the abscess drains into the bronchus, and the cough is dry
questions.exp: The clinical bullets read 'Fever, chills (Toxicity decreases on drainage into bronchus)' and 'Cough with purulent sputum'. (Book p289)

questions.sec: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture
questions.q: Which four examination findings are printed for a lung abscess?
opts: Tachypnea, impaired percussion, absent breath sounds and peripheral edema
Tachypnea, impaired percussion, cavity-related bronchial breathing and clubbing in a chronic abscess
Bradypnea, impaired percussion, cavity-related bronchial breathing and clubbing in acute abscess
Tachypnea, hyper-resonant percussion, cavity-related bronchial breathing and clubbing in chronic abscess
questions.exp: The O/E list reads 'Tachypnea, impaired percussion', 'Cavity related bronchial breathing' and 'Clubbing: In chronic abscess'. (Book p289)

questions.sec: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture
questions.q: Which diagnostic sequence is printed under Diagnosis on page 289?

Pneumonia with poor response to treatment over 2–3 days, then dry cough, with CT showing a ground glass opacity
Pneumonia with poor response to treatment over 2–3 days, then purulent sputum and toxicity, with a chest X-ray or CT showing an air fluid level
Pneumonia with rapid response to treatment, then hemoptysis, with a chest X-ray showing an air fluid level
questions.exp: The clinical line reads 'Pneumonia with poor response to Rx → 2-3 days → Purulent sputum → Toxicity', and the imaging line 'Chest X-ray/CT: Air fluid level'. (Book p289)

questions.sec: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture
questions.q: A patient with poor dentition and episodes of reduced consciousness develops a chronic abscess in the posterior segment of the upper lobe. Which cause and organism does the page print?
opts: Necrotising pneumonia with Staphylococcus
Aspiration pneumonia with anaerobes
Necrotising pneumonia with anaerobes
Aspiration pneumonia with Klebsiella
questions.exp: Aspiration pneumonia presents with chronic symptoms, anaerobes and a posterior upper lobe site that outranks the superior lower lobe segment; staphylococcus and klebsiella belong to necrotising pneumonia. (Book p289)

questions.sec: The Chest Film and CT Captions, Metastatic Infection to AA Amyloidosis, the Tuberculosis and Malignancy Differentials and the Vancomycin-Piperacillin-Tazobactam-Clindamycin Regimen

units.title: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
units.sec: Mycoplasma as the Smallest Free-Living Organism, Its Wall-Free Sterol Membrane, the Ten Percent Pneumonia Picture, Seven Extrapulmonary Manifestations, Radiology, PPLO Culture and Azithromycin
units.guide:
Mycoplasma (p286) is the smallest free-living replicating organism, with no cell wall so β-lactams fail, sterols present and no flagella; it causes tracheobronchitis/pharyngitis and pneumonia in 10%, spread by droplets, with low grade fever, cough, scanty sputum and few signs.
Extrapulmonary disease covers cold antibody autoimmune hemolysis (IgM), SJS/erythema multiforme, GBS, encephalitis, bullous myringitis, myocarditis/pericarditis and arthralgia with adenopathy; imaging gives reticulonodular or patchy consolidation from the hilum, interstitial and ground glass change and tree-in-bud.
PCR of respiratory secretions and serology are rapid and most sensitive, culture is on PPLO agar by Diene's method with fried egg colonies, and azithromycin is DOC with doxycycline and respiratory quinolones as alternatives; hydrogen peroxide and superoxide injure the epithelium but prognosis is good.

units.title: Chlamydia as an Obligate Intracellular Peptidoglycan-Free Bacterium with Its Elementary Body, Walking Pneumonia, HEp-2 Isolation and Micro-Immunofluorescence, plus the Legionella Phenotype
units.sec: Chlamydia as an Obligate Intracellular Peptidoglycan-Free Bacterium with Its Elementary Body, Walking Pneumonia, HEp-2 Isolation and Micro-Immunofluorescence, plus the Legionella Phenotype
units.guide:
Chlamydia (p287) is an obligate intracellular bacterium without peptidoglycan, transmitted human to human, its elementary body being extracellular, metabolically inactive and infective.
It gives a prolonged asymptomatic upper respiratory illness, atypical pneumonia in 10% and walking pneumonia indistinguishable from mycoplasma, with low grade fever, minimal sputum and dry cough, atherosclerosis being the extrapulmonary link; isolation is by HEp-2 cells and micro-immunofluorescence serology is the gold standard, with no lobar consolidation, resistance to sulfonamide and treatment by azithromycin or doxycycline.
Legionella is gram negative and predominantly intracellular, a strict aerobe, motile, partially acid fast, living in aquatic bodies and biofilms, with type 1 serovar most pathogenic and a type 4 secretion system.

units.title: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
units.sec: Legionella Microaspiration, BCYE Medium, the Sterile Gram Stain, Its Four Risk Factors, Typical against Atypical Disease, Pontiac against Legionnaires and DFAT Diagnosis
units.guide:
Legionella spreads by microaspiration more than aerosolization and grows on BCYE (buffered charcoal yeast extract) medium; Gram stain shows pus cells and neutrophils but no organisms (p288).
Risk factors are poor CMI, smoking, immunosuppression and hairy cell leukemia; typical disease is rapidly progressive with high grade fever, bilateral dense consolidation and leucocytosis, while atypical disease gives non-productive cough, diarrhea, hyponatremia, elevated LFT, thrombocytopenia and hematuria; mild disease is Pontiac fever and severe is Legionnaires disease.
DFAT and urinary antigen both have high specificity, sputum/aspiration testing is not done, and treatment is azithromycin (DOC) with rifampicin or a quinolone.

units.title: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture
units.sec: Necrotising Pneumonia and Aspiration as the Two Causes of Lung Abscess, the Five-Step Pathogenesis, the Posterior Right Upper Lobe Site and the Clinical Picture
units.guide:
Lung abscess (p289) has two causes: necrotising pneumonia complicating pneumonia from staphylococcus or klebsiella, and aspiration pneumonia with chronic symptoms, anaerobes and a posterior upper lobe predilection over the superior lower lobe segment.
Pathogenesis runs consolidation + suppuration + necrosis → rupture → drainage into the bronchus → purulent expectoration → abscess with an air fluid level, the commonest site being the posterior segment of the right upper lobe.
Clinically fever and chills ease when the abscess drains, with cough and purulent sputum, tachypnea, impaired percussion, cavity-related bronchial breathing and clubbing in chronic disease; diagnosis is poor response over 2–3 days with purulent sputum and toxicity plus an air fluid level on film or CT.

units.title: The Chest Film and CT Captions, Metastatic Infection to AA Amyloidosis, the Tuberculosis and Malignancy Differentials and the Vancomycin-Piperacillin-Tazobactam-Clindamycin Regimen
units.sec: The Chest Film and CT Captions, Metastatic Infection to AA Amyloidosis, the Tuberculosis and Malignancy Differentials and the Vancomycin-Piperacillin-Tazobactam-Clindamycin Regimen
units.guide:
Captions on p290 run ground glass opacity, pleural effusion, thick walled cavity, consolidation and air fluid levels.
Complications are metastatic infection, pyopneumothorax, bronchopleural fistula and AA (secondary) amyloidosis, the last seen in TB, bronchiectasis and lung abscess; the differential is TB, malignancy, Nocardia and Actinomycetes with no bracketed clue.
Treatment is antibiotics with postural drainage — vancomycin, piperacillin–tazobactam and clindamycin for anaerobes — for 6–8 weeks, fever resolving in 7–10 days and surgery reserved for unresponsive MDR disease.

units.title: The Three Severely Immunocompromised States, the Seven Organisms, and the Renal and Bone Marrow Transplant Infection Timelines with Onset-Based Infection
units.sec: The Three Severely Immunocompromised States, the Seven Organisms, and the Renal and Bone Marrow Transplant Infection Timelines with Onset-Based Infection
units.guide:
The severely immunocompromised (p291) are neutropenic from any cause, transplant recipients of bone marrow or kidney, and those on >30 mg steroid for 3–4 weeks; organisms are mainly MDR gram-negative with Aspergillus, Nocardia and PCP predominant in the lung, plus toxoplasma, CMV and candida.
Post renal transplant: <1 month wound, catheter, drain site, UTI and herpes; 1–6 months (m/c) CMV, PCP, Legionella, Listeria and hepatitis B/C; >6 months drug-induced neutropenia from mycophenolate or calcineurin inhibitors giving BK polyoma, Nocardia and Aspergillus.
Post bone marrow transplant: <1 month gram-negative bacteria and Aspergillus, then 1–4 months CMV, PCP and Aspergillus; acute onset at 24–48 hours means bacteria, subacute means virus, TB or fungi, with CMV ocular/organomegaly, Nocardia neurological/nodules and Pseudomonas ecthyma gangrenosum.

units.title: Invasive Aspergillosis from Conidia to Hyphae, Neutropenia as the Chief Risk, the Halo and Air Crescent Signs, the Reverse Halo and Monad Notes and the Fever-Hemoptysis-Pleuritic Triad
units.sec: Invasive Aspergillosis from Conidia to Hyphae, Neutropenia as the Chief Risk, the Halo and Air Crescent Signs, the Reverse Halo and Monad Notes and the Fever-Hemoptysis-Pleuritic Triad
units.guide:
Invasive aspergillosis (p292) starts with conidia aerosolised from the mold, reaching tissue and forming invasive hyphae, with neutropenia the most important risk.
The CT halo sign is consolidation surrounded by ground glass and suggests invasion, while the air crescent sign means recovery; the reverse halo is ground glass surrounded by consolidation in cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, and the monad sign is an air crescent around a fungal ball that moves with posture in an old TB aspergilloma.
The classical triad is fever, hemoptysis and pleuritic pain, with sinus infection, CNS infection carrying 100% mortality and angioinvasion causing hemorrhagic infarction.

units.title: Aspergillus Diagnosis by BAL, VATS and Galactomannan, Beta-D-Glucan Cross-Reactivity, Voriconazole against Liposomal Amphotericin, the Mucormycosis Contrast and the Opening of Pneumocystis
units.sec: Aspergillus Diagnosis by BAL, VATS and Galactomannan, Beta-D-Glucan Cross-Reactivity, Voriconazole against Liposomal Amphotericin, the Mucormycosis Contrast and the Opening of Pneumocystis
units.guide:
Diagnosis of aspergillosis (p293) rests on BAL showing dichotomous branching septate hyphae, VATS biopsy of a nodule, the specific galactomannan test and β-D-glucan, which is positive in mucor, cryptococcus, candida, aspergillosis and pneumocystis.
Voriconazole is DOC with liposomal amphotericin B as the alternative, and mucormycosis is separated by aseptate right-angle hyphae, negative galactomannan, no voriconazole response and treatment with liposomal amphotericin B plus posaconazole and surgical debridement.
Pneumocystis is a fungal infection of HIV with CD4 <200/μL and the immunocompromised, giving dyspnea and hypoxia then fever and cough after 2–3 days.

units.title: Pneumocystis Diagnosis by GMS Cyst Stain, Fluorescein Antibody and PCR, Its Four HIV Records, the Cotrimoxazole Ladder, Steroids for Hypoxia and Three Prophylactic Drugs
units.sec: Pneumocystis Diagnosis by GMS Cyst Stain, Fluorescein Antibody and PCR, Its Four HIV Records, the Cotrimoxazole Ladder, Steroids for Hypoxia and Three Prophylactic Drugs
units.guide:
Pneumocystis diagnosis (p294) uses a positive but non-specific 1,3 β-D-glucan, raised LDH, BAL microscopy as the best mode with GMS cyst staining, fluorescein conjugated monoclonal antibody, PCR as gold standard and perihilar infiltrates that may cavitate, pneumothorax or pneumatocele.
It is the most common fungal pneumonia, opportunistic infection, cause of pneumonia and cause of pleural effusion in HIV; treatment is oral cotrimoxazole for mild-moderate disease, IV cotrimoxazole for severe, and second line clindamycin + primaquine or IV pentamidine.
Steroids are added for PaO₂ <70 mm Hg or a raised arterio-alveolar gradient, and prophylaxis is cotrimoxazole, dapsone or atovaquone.

units.title: Nocardia asteroides as an Aerobic Acid-Fast Filamentous Organism, Its Mandatory Host Defect, Brain and Lung Disease, the Crooked Beaded Filaments and the Sulfonamide Regimen
units.sec: Nocardia asteroides as an Aerobic Acid-Fast Filamentous Organism, Its Mandatory Host Defect, Brain and Lung Disease, the Crooked Beaded Filaments and the Sulfonamide Regimen
units.guide:
Nocardia asteroides (p295) is a gram positive filamentous 'fungus' that is aerobic, acid fast and filamented, unlike non-acid-fast non-aerobic actinomycetes and acid-fast non-filamentous rhodococci.
A host defence defect is mandatory, entry is by inhalation or a skin defect, and disease is a subacute brain abscess or cavitating lung nodules with nocardial mycetoma.
Sputum or pus shows acid-fast crooked branching beaded filaments and culture is avoided because of slow growth; treatment is sulfonamide as DOC with minocycline and parenteral amikacin.
